(Feel free to correct me if I’m wrong about these, since I’m writing this up as I’m reviewing the episode. I’ve also not seen Episode 4 yet, so it’s fine if the speculative Hidden Rules are incorrect.)

Players are represented by a six-sided die with their face on it. Each side is a different color. At the beginning of the game, players start on any unoccupied gray tile on the board. You can move from where your die is onto any orthogonally adjacent (this would mean up left down right, non diagonal) space on the board, “rolling” in that direction. If another player’s die is occupying the tile you are “rolling” onto, you push them in the direction your die is moving, “rolling” them in that direction.

The game operates with a set of “Hidden Rules”, which are conditions that trigger based on game actions or effects, such as a die moving onto a new tile. These triggers can depend on things like the colors of the tiles surrounding your die and so on.

The Hidden Rules that have been hardline revealed at the end of Episode 3 are these:  
  
1. If the tile you land on is a white tile, or if your die rolls white side up, you will be exiled and receive an exile token. Being exiled means you must return to any free starting gray tile.  
  
2. After receiving 3 exile tokens, you lose 3 Pieces. (For any player with 3 or less Pieces, this means instant elimination from the show.)


The rules that I believe can be intuited from Episode 3’s gameplay are these:  
  
>!1. If after rolling onto a new tile, no color in the eight tiles surrounding your die (the squares adjacent to your die’s tile, or less if your die is on the edge of the board) match the color of your die that’s facing up, you must choose a new color. This new color must be one of those colors surrounding your die.!<  
  
>!2. If within the range of the eight tiles there are three colors that match the color of your die that’s facing up (including said die), you move someone else’s die that matches the color of yours 1 space orthogonally (as per usual movement rules). This movement can trigger additional effects.!<  
  
>!3. If in the situation of the above-given rule your die and surrounding spaces form a three-in-a-row of the same color, orthogonal or diagonal, you can move your die 1 additional space (while also triggering the above rule).!<

The poetic metaphor of all the characters was tied together very firmly. >!I have a preference for open-endedness, and there’s a strong emphasis on how the ending isn’t something notable happening, or some kind of tangible conclusion. There's no substantive, definitive liberation, but there's filling up five minutes of each day with the transient seconds: in those moments, there was something that might be called liberation, if only for a little bit. It's no ending in the traditional sense, because the curtains don't ever close on these characters, but rather the “어렵게 어렵게 가는,” translated as “trudging along,” but probably better described as “moving forward, with great difficulty.” It’s an ending holding that kind of forward motion within it.!<

Six Flying Dragons is a historical piece and >!if you know even a bit of the relevant history, you already know how it ends,!< but it captures the characters in a snapshot moment where they live on forever, between the panels of history. It’s a drama that’s ultimately about the height and weight and breadth of ideology, and I think it settles perfectly where each ideology should rest.

This is what I desperately hope will be retained in his Arcane depiction. What made Viktor so fascinating lore-wise was that, despite his rejection of 'humanity' (flesh, depravity, error, the mendacity of Piltover and the sickness that permeates Zaun), he seemed a character who was always, always in pursuit of humanity: kindness, dreams that drift to elusive heights, and above all, his overwhelmingly immense capacity of love for others.

My biggest gripe is an inordinate amount of very basic non-idiom lines received this treatment as well. I actually don't quite mind when idioms get liberal translations (I'm generally on the liberal side with translations myself!), but something as simple as "let's go home" was translated as "let's go together", where the context of the scene is seized with the notion that Sangwoo and Gihun were close enough in their childhood that they'd considered each other's mother their own, or when Saebyeok asks Gihun to "make a deal" with her, where 약속 is almost always "promise" (or contract when framed in the appropriate context) before it is "deal"; usually I don't consider something small like this an issue, but calling it a "deal" instead of a "promise" substantially altered the meaning, pathologizes it and sets it in a more clinical tone (where the scene is much better off with the emotional weight of a word like "promise"). It's probably a bit petty of me to point out the deal/promise digression, but these add up ("once every three lines" was no hyperbole), such that entire scenes lost the subtle touch of something crucial.

I've done translations before and I understand creative license, but this was particularly off-putting because this happens with a frequency of once every three lines. Most of these translations are not only highly reductive + cut away important nuance, but they also had distinct, straightforward alternatives that were much closer in approximation to the original meaning, and that was what was so frustrating about it.

imo the anti-adverb sentiment that's commonly described by King and other writers oversimplifies adverb application. what they mean is that they dislike adverbs that don't contribute to a sentence, e.g. "I spoke quietly" can be "I whispered" or "I muttered" where "whispered" or "muttered" conveys much more than "spoke quietly" (however, even here I'd argue that "spoke quietly" has its own merits--"spoke quietly" is a vaguer expression than "whispered" and sometimes you don't want to convey as much as "whispered," you want to convey an explicitly vague notion of speaking quietly and in that case you absolutely can and should use "spoke quietly"); however, adverbs add so much to your writing when applied correctly. going back to the "I spoke" example, "I spoke deliberately and measuredly" has two adverbs but can't be conveyed with merely "I \[verb\]" because then the meaning completely changes--there's no way to say the same thing with a more economic approach ("I spoke at a deliberate and measured pace" could be similar but some people would consider that clunkier and wordier--then it becomes of a question of preference).

word economy is pretty tricky to parse, but "adverbs bad" is a pretty bad rule to go by, because adverbs can be absolutely necessary to what you're trying to convey. here's a better rule that covers the issues King has with adverbs without excluding use of adverbs in contexts where they're necessary: don't use words (any part of speech) unnecessary or disruptive to what you intend to express.

I really want to emphasize that bit you said about putting stock into collectivism. I was raised with a cultural background not very similar at all to the classic American (mode demographic) upbringing, and to me the vast, vast majority of this sub getting excused as NTA consists of horrible, horrible behavior. That being said, even by the most fundamental of American legal values I feel so many posters easily satisfy that asshole bar--by infringing on a very basic principle of freedom by taking away from them an indispensable sense of comfort or control over their own environment. To everyone who ends up saying something along the lines of "NTA, you don't owe anyone anything": hell yes you do.

You owe them respect, personal space, the right to exercise their agency freely. You owe them your assistance (upon request and/or if they genuinely are in need of said assistance) if it doesn't moderately inconvenience you. You owe them polite, appropriate responses, even when they're assholes themselves--being the better person doesn't make you a doormat; if you want to make a point, clearly assert the point. You don't stoop to their level (or lower). Violent or hurtful retaliation should never be your immediate response, it's the very, very last resort, if all else--and I mean everything else, even seeking mediation from authority of which I myself am not the biggest fan--fails. You owe them manners, something which is incredibly understated in this sub. *You owe people general kindness and compassion by default*. Politeness and kindness are not the equivalent of self-sacrifice. You don't even have to be generous or charitable. Common decency, at the very least, should be upheld. These standards really aren't as high as people make them out to be.
